lesson.section: 26. Pelvic Girdle and Hip Bone Landmarks

steps.title: Pelvic Girdle and Hip Bone Landmarks
steps.body: The pelvic girdle consists of right hip bone, left hip bone, sacrum, and coccyx. Each hip bone is made of ilium, ischium, and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Important landmarks: iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, greater and lesser sciatic notches, obturator foramen, acetabulum. Greater and lesser sciatic notches are converted into foramina by sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments. Obturator foramen is closed mostly by obturator membrane. Acetabulum receives the femoral head.

steps.title: How does the sacroiliac region transfer load toward the lower limbs?
steps.body: The sacrum receives axial load from the vertebral column and transmits it through sacroiliac articulations and strong ligamentous supports to the hip bones. The pelvic ring distributes force toward acetabula and femora. The pubic symphysis completes the anterior connection but is not the sole load-bearing bridge. This ring structure means forces at one location affect neighboring connections. On a pelvic diagram, show sacrum, both sacroiliac joints, acetabula and symphysis together rather than learning each landmark without the load pathway.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Ilium, ischium and pubis meet around the acetabulum. The acetabular fossa is central and non-articular, while the lunate surface bears articular cartilage. The obturator foramen is largely closed by membrane, leaving a canal for the obturator neurovascular bundle. Ischial spine and tuberosity are different landmarks: the spine helps orient pelvic nerve routes, the tuberosity supports sitting and anchors muscles. A named prominence should be linked to its function and neighboring route.
